messages.subject: Is there a zero inflation problem with mark recapture models?
messages.subject_clean: Is there a zero inflation problem with mark recapture models?
messages.body_plain:
I'm wondering if it could be a problem for a CJS model when you have a lot of individuals that were seen only once and never seen again (e.g. 001000 or 100000 etc. vs 110000 or 001110 etc.)

if you have 1300 lines in your capture history where an individual has been seen only once compared to >2 times have only 500 lines, is it biasing your survival or recapture rate estimates?

Is it possible to delete all the 1300 lines containing only one capture and no recapture?

messages.subject: AW: Is there a zero inflation problem with mark recapture models?
messages.subject_clean: AW: Is there a zero inflation problem with mark recapture models?
messages.body_plain:
It’s possible that there are transients in the data (individuals that are present in the study area only at one occasion) or that survival has an age structure with juvenile survival being lower than adult survival. Classical goodness-of-fit test as can be done in U-CARE are indicative about these potential problems. Models exist that can account for transients or that have an age structure (see e.g. the paper by Roger Pradel (1997) in Biometrics). Deleting the capture histories of all individual captured only once is wrong and would result in a positive bias of the estimate of survival.

messages.subject_clean: Is there a zero inflation problem with mark recapture models?
messages.body_plain:
[sending now to the whole list]

this could be a problem of transience  which can be dealt with using a zero-inflation type of a model.  There are quite a few papers on modeling transience, I think some of them are cited in the Royle and Dorazio (2008) book around p 363. I think Pradel et al. (1997) and Hines et al. (2003).   The basic idea is you introduce a latent parameter R_{I} = 1 if resident 0 otherwise and R_{I} ~ Bern(theta) or something, and then the CJS model applies to the R_{I} = 1 individuals.
I imagine Kery and Schaub talk about this in the BPA book too or cite some references but I can't remember.
regards
andy

messages.subject: appropriate alpha values for the Dirichlet distribution
messages.subject_clean: appropriate alpha values for the Dirichlet distribution
messages.body_plain:
Hello all:

I've done some searching on other internet forums for information on the Dirichlet distribution, with answers seemingly over my head or not relevant to my needs (or both).  I thought it would be appropriate to post here on the HMEcology forum; advance apologies if it is not.

I am fitting a multinomial model in WinBUGS, and using a Dirichlet prior.  McCarthy (Bayesian Methods for Ecology) has a nice write-up on the Dirichlet for novices like me (p. 274 of his book) but it is not clear to me what reasonable values for the alpha's might be for a non-informative prior.  In model fits to dummy data I have used alpha values ranging from 0.2 to 2, with essentially identical results.

Thank you, Paul Rudershausen

messages.subject: AW: direct recovery coding in state-space model (BAP Chp.8)
messages.subject_clean: AW: direct recovery coding in state-space model (BAP Chp.8)
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tim,

No worries about the spelling of BPA...

Regarding coding the capture-histories for a band recovery model: if an animal is marked and found dead in the same year, the capture history fragment gets 11. This means that the individual was released alive at occasion t and recovered dead at occasion t+1 (actually, since there is usually not a short and well defined recovery period, it means that the animal was found dead some when between release ccasion t and release occasion t+1), hence the probability of this fragment gets (1-s[t])*r[t]. You are right that in MARK the coding is different, because there are for each occasion two columns, one for the release and one for the potential recovery. In the actual case the recovery would also be at occasion t. The different coding has no effect on the parameter estimates, but the labelling of the recovery parameters is different.

Kind regards

Michael

Spatial Capture-Recapture Workshop in Banff

Instructors
Andy Royle (USGS Patuxent Wildlife Research Center)
Richard Chandler (University of Georgia)
Angela Fuller (USGS and Cornell University)

Date: 12-14 March 2018 (3 days)

Location: Banff, Canada

Cost
USD$600 (normal rate) or USD$450 (student rate). Cost includes
breakfast, lunch, and refreshment breaks.

Overview
This course introduces key models used in the analysis of
spatially-explicit capture-recapture data using Bayesian and classical
(likelihood) methods. It closely follows material from the book
"Spatial Capture-Recapture" (Elsevier, 2014). The workshop will cover
basic model and data analysis concepts in R and the BUGS language
(using WinBUGS or JAGS), analysis of classical capture-recapture
models (models M0, Mb, Mh, etc...), concepts and methods of spatial
capture-recapture models and their analysis using the R package "oSCR"
and also using the BUGS language. Advanced topics will include open
population models and integrated population models.

Registration
Registration information and additional information about the workshop
can be found here: http://conted.warnell.uga.edu/courses/cap-recap2018

messages.subject: comparing models with first-order and second-order Markov processes
messages.subject_clean: comparing models with first-order and second-order Markov processes
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I've got a multi-state model where we are exploring nth-order Markov processes for breeding site presence, given a breeding interval >2 yrs.  For example, a female with offspring could conceivably not return to the breeding site for 3 years, so the history of partially latent breeding site presences needs to go beyond t-1.  This is referred to as a "memory model" in MARK, though MARK cannot actually fit models beyond a first-order Markov process.  This is trivial in JAGS.

The problem I am having is with model comparison, as it is not clear which metrics can be used to compare models with a Markovian dependence that is first-order vs. second-order, etc.  I tried including the breeding interval as a random variable, but the chains get stuck at initial values and do not mix (unsurprisingly).  The problem is that the models condition on more and more latent states as you go up in order, so of course things like deviance are going to increase.

As it stands, the second-order model has the greatest separation between probabilities of breeding site presence for individuals that were present in years t-1 or t-2, and those that were not.  Maybe this is the best I can do...

Just curious if anyone has addressed this problem, particularly in the literature.  The issue should be the same for spatial CAR processes, so it would seem to be a fairly general problem.  Would be nice if there is something I've overlooked.

Thanks,
Dan

messages.subject: Problems with CJS models in m-array formulation with only one cohort
messages.subject_clean: Problems with CJS models in m-array formulation with only one cohort
messages.body_plain:
Good morning,

I am trying to implement CJS models in marray formulation but I am using capture-recapture data with individuals ringed only the first year of the study. When I try to construct the marray following the code by Kèry and Schaub 2012 and I run the model (the simplest one, constant effects) the results are wrong. I think the problem is the marray itself. Is it possible that with only one cohort I cannot use marray formulation? I have seven years of recapture.

Any help will be appreciated,

Blanca

messages.subject: tricks for constraining hyperparameter values to yield plausible survival/recovery values
messages.subject_clean: tricks for constraining hyperparameter values to yield plausible survival/recovery values
messages.body_plain:
I'm still working on a recovery model, now including hyperparameters. I'd like to try to set my priors to exclude unrealsitic survival or recovery parameters. I know it doesn't matter much once you have a lot of data, but it's still something I'd like to play around with. Without hyperparameters, I've had success, using truncated, beta, or normal distributions with larger-than-typical precision values. I was just curious if any one had any luck doing this with hyperparameters and if you had any tricks for distributions or mean/precision/shape parameter values.

Thanks
